raw_segments.text: The hog, that finds his food among order, and greedily devours many things rejected
by every other useful animal, is, like poultry, originally kept as a save-all.
As long as the number of such animals, which can thus be reared at little or no expense,
is fully sufficient to supply the demand, this sort of butcher's meat comes to market
at a much lower price than any other.
But when the demand rises beyond what this quantity can supply, when it becomes necessary
to raise food on purpose for feeding and fattening hogs, in the same manner as for feeding and
fattening other cattle, the price necessarily rises, and becomes proportionably either higher
or lower than that of other butcher's meat, according as the nature of the country, and
the state of its agriculture, happen to render the feeding of hogs more or less expensive
In France, according to Mr. Buffon, the price of pork is nearly equal to that of beef.
In most parts of Great Britain, it is, at present, somewhat higher.
